title: Chapter 7 | Emergent Intelligence Beyond Biology
text: CHAPTER 7 Emergent Intelligence Beyond Biology The internet began generating oceans of digital data. Graphics Processing Units or GPUs—originally designed for the high-speed rendering required in video game graphics—turned out to be perfect for parallel processing in neural networks. Unlike Central Processing Units or CPUs, which excel at a few complex operations at a time, GPUs run thousands of simple operations in parallel—the exact pattern needed to train large neural nets efficiently. By far the leader in this space is the Wall Street darling, NVIDIA, which recently ballooned into one of the world’s most valuable companies as others worked to catch up. NVIDIA Provides the Engine of AI Founded in 1993 by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem, NVIDIA began as a niche graphics card manufacturer focused on the emerging video game market. What set the company apart wasn’t just hardware—it was vision. Huang, who immigrated from Taiwan and worked as a dishwasher in his youth, has often said that what matters isn’t the job but how you do the job. He describes his desire in that job to be the best dishwasher ever. That relentless pursuit of excellence—combined with long-range thinking—became the cultural backbone of the company. Under Huang’s leadership, NVIDIA made a critical bet: that the same GPU chips used to accelerate graphics rendering for gamers could be repurposed for general purpose parallel processing. It was a bold move at the time, but it proved visionary. By the 2010s, as machine learning began to explode, it became clear that neural networks required vast amounts of parallel computation. NVIDIA’s GPUs were perfectly suited. Seemingly overnight, NVIDIA wasn’t just a gaming chip company—it became the default provider of AI infrastructure. Today, NVIDIA powers everything from autonomous vehicles to supercomputers to generative AI platforms such as ChatGPT. Its stock price soared, and Huang has become one of the most admired leaders in tech. Geoffrey Hinton, the “Godfather of AI” Back to Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, often called the Godfather of AI, who spent decades championing neural networks even when the field dismissed them, eventually leading to the breakthrough that ignited modern AI. He didn’t just imagine machines that could compute—he imagined machines that could learn in ways inspired by biology. His persistence paid off with AlexNet. In 2012, AlexNet, the system built by Hinton and his students, crushed the ImageNet visual recognition challenge using a deep convolutional neural network. It was the spark that reignited the field. Later recruited by Google, Hinton’s work laid the conceptual and architectural foundation for today’s deep learning systems. The breakthrough wasn’t about better logic. It was about brute force learning: Show a network millions of examples, let it make billions of mistakes, and it will eventually predict with uncanny accuracy. The success of AlexNet led directly to Google’s acquisition of DeepMind, the development of systems such as AlphaGo, and the modern deep learning revolution. What changed? The model, yes. But more than that, it was the injection of large amounts of energy and access to massive data using this incredible layered learning architecture idea, which originally evolved in the human brain under the shaping force of energy constraint. Early AI models failed in part because they didn’t mimic how we learn. But they also failed because they were underpowered—literally. Today’s deep neural networks are not just intelligent because they are more elegant and leverage how our brains learn. They are also intelligent because they are fueled. They draw on massive computational resources to radically scale the kind of localized pattern recognition our brains perform with a fraction of the energy. Human Memory Storage and AI Vector Databases As we encounter new experiences, observations, or facts and process them in a sequence of escalating layers of prediction and response, the hippocampus is engaged to determine when something new has occurred that should be updated in the memory system. And the new data only gets to the hippocampus if it contradicts expectations all the way up the chain. The filtering is the continuous discarding of all the lower, faster levels of prediction and response. But here’s a notable part: Most things are not stored. The hippocampus must make constant value judgments about the new information’s future worth. The brain is constantly filtering—deciding which inputs merit energy investment for long-term encoding. This decision is heavily influenced by relevance, novelty, and emotion. If something doesn’t matter or doesn’t move us, it’s typically discarded. If it does matter—especially if it carries emotional weight—it passes through the hippocampus and is distributed to other parts of the brain during sleep for integration into long-term memory. This distribution is mapped to relevant other memories (neurons) for fast retrieval and association. This principle—relevance, association, and distributed encoding—appears in an analogous way in artificial intelligence. The comparison is functional, not architectural. Vector Databases in AI In a vector database, each memory or piece of data is encoded as a high-dimensional vector: a string of numbers that mathematically captures its semantic meaning . On its surface, vector databases seem foreign and complex, in that information is converted into long strings of numbers that, to the human mind without a code key, are largely undecipherable. However, if you step back and consider the underlying function, modern AI vector databases organize and retrieve information in ways that might be understood to conceptually mirror how the brain accesses meaning through associative memory. Rather than being sorted by strict labels or categories, these data points are stored by proximity of meaning in multidimensional space. When you query a vector database, it doesn’t return only the exact match—it returns the closest meanings based on context and learned associations. If traditional databases are a card catalog (exact matches), vector databases are a librarian who knows that king and queen are related not by spelling but by the concept of royalty . Certainly, when we think about the massive web of our neurons in our biological brains firing electrical signals in the storage or retrieval of information, that is as equally nonintuitive as a long string of numbers in a vector database. Similarly, human memory works through associations rather than strict categorization. When we try to recall a fact, we don’t sort through a mental filing cabinet; we activate related concepts, emotional connections, and narrative contexts. Both biological and artificial systems use networks of associations. When we try to recall a fact, we don’t sort through a list alphabetically—we remember related things, emotionally charged moments, stories that stuck. Our brain doesn’t store data in strict files; it creates an interwoven web of meaning, dynamically accessed depending on context. While not architecturally or structurally the same, vector databases offer a conceptual parallel to how the brain organizes memory—by proximity of meaning. The work at our learning company has centered on helping people generate deeply integrated enduring memory with extraordinary efficiency. Understanding how the brain encodes memory has guided both the scientific and technological approaches we’ve taken. And today, we have nearly six billion learner interactions in our platform. This is a giant database of behavior. And the findings from that database are then deeply integrated into our AI training agent and loaded into the AI brain, its vector database. But to fully appreciate this parallel, it helps to look deeper inside the AI itself. In transformer-based neural networks such as ChatGPT, once the input text is tokenized and converted to high-dimensional vectors, it is passed through a series of layered processing blocks—often dozens or even hundreds deep. Each layer contains mechanisms for attention (which allows the model to focus on relevant context) and feed-forward transformation (which distills that context into new representations). You can visualize these layers like stacked systems of filters and pathways—a cascade where each level reinterprets the prior one, enhancing abstraction and refining meaning. At every step, attention flows backward and forward, emphasizing context and forming the basis for predictive reasoning. This structure resembles the cortical feedback loops in the human brain that we talked about in the section called “The Layered Brain” (no, that is just a coconut, not a face), where information flows not just forward from sensory input to higher cognition but also backward, allowing memory, expectation, and intention to shape perception. Feedback loops allow expectations to influence how ambiguous signals are resolved. And aligning with expectations can be more convincing to the brain than reality itself. Similarly, in generative pretrained transformer (GPT) models, early layers might detect sentence structure, while deeper layers infer tone, intent, or even contradiction, feeding back those insights into the unfolding prediction process. Both systems demonstrate that intelligence doesn’t arise from static storage. It emerges from the dynamic interplay of layers, where prediction, context, and memory converge to construct meaning. When GPT completes your sentence, or your brain recalls a childhood memory in the middle of a conversation, the underlying mechanisms—though materially different—are functionally resonant. It’s not that GPT is a brain. It’s that both are systems for layered inference, association, and predictive construction. Each layer refines and reshapes meaning in a way that allows thought—or output—to feel coherent, connected, and alive. And the resulting relational storage in a vector database feels highly analogous to the famous principle about our brains’ storage and retrieval. Based on the foundational work of neuroscientist Donald Hebb, Stanford neuroscientist Carla Shatz coined the memorable phrase: 33 , 34 “Neurons that fire together, wire together.” And that is the point we are trying to grasp here. Both biological and artificial neurons that fire together do indeed wire together to form what we call meaning. Revisiting the Role of Confidence in Human Learning In AI, a “hallucination” occurs when the model produces an answer with an expression of high “confidence,” despite lacking a factual basis. It is striking how efforts to mitigate hallucinations in large language models echo the processes of human learning. We explored how prompting learners on our platform to assess their confidence during learning heightened attention and dramatically improved understanding and retention of new knowledge. This metacognitive act required engagement of the amygdala—the brain region linked to emotional salience and decision-making that we talked about—effectively priming the brain to pay closer attention and integrate learning more deeply. Researchers had to train the AI by modeling the idea that it was acceptable for the AI not to know, introducing a form of internal “confidence” estimation. This allowed the model to say, in effect, “I’m unsure.” Once that foundational behavior was working, the next step was to give the AI tools the ability to pause, conduct a real-time search for relevant information, incorporate that new data into its context window, and then generate a revised and more informed response. This sequence mirrors the human process: becoming aware of a gap in understanding, seeking external input, and returning with new clarity. It reinforces the idea that both biological and artificial systems thrive best when they have a functional mechanism for assessing their knowledge, recognizing when they don’t know, and knowing how to respond next. We will discuss the biological version of AI hallucinations, the breakdown of this metacognitive step, a bit later when we discuss the Dunning–Kruger effect. Just as a human learner becomes more attentive when uncertain or when they discover that they were confident and wrong, AI systems are being taught to pause when “confidence” is low. But the parallel goes further. Rather than simply accepting the gap, the model is trained to seek: to initiate a real-time search—often across the web—for new information that might clarify or resolve the uncertainty. Once that additional context is retrieved, it is integrated into the model’s working memory and used to generate a more informed response. In essence, the AI learns to recognize its limitations, activate external inquiry, and then revisit the task with an expanded awareness. This process—pause, search, integrate, respond—is not unlike the recursive way humans deepen understanding through curiosity, exploration, and reflection. As with human cognition, intelligence here is not defined by always knowing the answer but by knowing how to respond when you don’t. As we continue, we’ll explore how these memory systems—both human and artificial—are not just about storage. They are about construction. They are active, dynamic— predictive . And in both systems, memory is not passive—it is a central element of intelligence . The Emergence of Something Different Biological brains, forged by evolution and refined by necessity, have been our only known locus of thought, imagination, and creativity. Intelligence, as we understood it, was biological and embodied by definition. It breathed, it blinked, it aged. And then, suddenly, it didn’t. When DeepMind’s AlphaGo AI defeated world champion Lee Sedol in 2016, something fundamental shifted. 35 This wasn’t mimicry. This was originality. It wasn’t just fast computing. It was simulating something that felt like intuition—born not of consciousness but of pattern. But we must be careful here. AlphaGo didn’t feel the joy of victory. It had no awareness. No curiosity. It was a savant without a soul. Still, it had proven something extraordinary: That intelligence is not exclusive to biological systems. And AlphaGo had no body. No life history. It was pure structure and energy. Intelligence had escaped biology. This was the first real sign that the emergence of high-level intelligence could exist outside a biological brain. And that’s the critical shift: • Human intelligence is constrained by fixed constraints of time, energy, biology, and other factors. • Artificial intelligence is constrained by architecture, training data, and compute. Chips get faster at an accelerating pace, throughput per chip is accelerating rapidly, and AI can be plugged into the power grid, increasing abundance rather than fixed constraint, while leveraging the findings of our biology hyperefficient intelligence evolution. Intelligence, once confined to biology and constraint, has found new fuel. Better at Sharing Hinton also famously states that AI is a better computational learning engine than humans because “they’re billions of times better than us at sharing information.” Let’s unpack that a bit. Imagine one million Tesla fully self-driving AI cars on the road. Each one engaged in the constraints of moving around in a messy and complex physical world. However, they are all connected to a central AI brain in addition to the AI in the individual car. Meaning, what one Tesla self-driving AI car learns, they all learn. As humans, we have not found a way to do that. If we are now no longer the only system in the universe capable of learning, the question then becomes: Are we the only ones capable of understanding? Understanding: The Compost and the Bomb “What do a compost heap and a nuclear bomb have in common?” It’s a question that, at first glance, seems absurd. One decomposes organic matter slowly; the other obliterates everything around it in an instant. When Geoffrey Hinton asked humans that question, the most common response was confusion or silence. But when Hinton asked this of an AI neural network—trained not only on language but on deep pattern association—it responded: “They are both uncontrolled chain reactions. That in both cases, an initiating event triggers a self-perpetuating cascade.” This was more than clever wordplay. It was an illustration of some form of pattern recognition that required a fairly high level of understanding to find. The model didn’t arrive at this insight by recalling a memorized phrase or through statistical next-word prediction alone. It synthesized an abstract connection by identifying a structural similarity. In both cases, a chain reaction is triggered where the output of one step becomes the fuel for the next. In a compost heap, microbial decomposition releases heat, which in turn accelerates further microbial activity, deepening the slow cycle of decay. In a nuclear bomb, the splitting of atomic nuclei releases neutrons, which then collide with other nuclei, causing them to split and release more energy in a runaway explosion. One is slow, organic, and life-giving. The other is instantaneous, engineered, and destructive. But both obey the same underlying principle: a chain reaction that compounds itself once set in motion. To Hinton, this response was profound. It suggested that the system had done more than mimic intelligence—it had exhibited a form of understanding . The AI was not simply regurgitating facts; it was drawing inferences across domains, compressing complexity into metaphor, and offering up a novel synthesis. In the context of our discussion, this matters deeply. It underscores a pivotal shift: The intelligence that we ignited in silicon is beginning to form its own models of the world. And that, as we’ve seen in our own brains, is where real learning—and real intelligence—begins to emerge. Now, I understand that some will say: “Exactly. This is a statistical generalization producing the appearance of insight.” Yes—of course. But that may be the point. Maybe, at some level, that’s what intelligence actually is, and all that is missing is consciousness. This, I believe, is what intelligence begins to look like when a system can reflect not only on content but on the form and function of communication itself. Maybe understanding is pattern recognition—but stretched across time with memory, structure, and intent. Which is why AI’s recent development of what appears like memory across your interactions is so profound. Understanding, as we’ve seen, emerges from pattern recognition across vast domains. But understanding without memory is fleeting—like a brilliant conversation that vanishes the moment it ends. What transformed AI from a clever pattern matcher into something approaching a true thought partner was the addition of something analogous to memory. OceanofPDF.com
